newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shorter workweek plan draws more criticism.
newsitem.headline: German shorter workweek plan draws more criticism.

text.p: German union leaders at the weekend defended a proposal to create new jobs by cutting back working hours while employers and commentators accused them of threatening Germany's global competitiveness.

Attacking IG Metall chief Klaus Zwickel's call to cut the working week to 32 hours, Hans Olaf Henkel, head of the Federation of German Industry (BDI) said the plan would do nothing to cut Germany's 11.7 percent jobless rate.

"This plan is totally ridiculous and belongs in a museum, we already have the world's lowest annual rate of hours worked. At the same time we have seen that the jobless rate has fallen in nations where people work more, not less," Henkel said in Monday's edition of German newspaper Leipziger Volksstimme.
In an opinion column in Sunday's mass circulation Bild am Sonntag, Alfred Merta said IG Metall risked taking a step backwards not forwards with its newest plan.
"A nation where people mostly want to work only 32 hours a week, will become the laughing stock of the world. The competition would love that," Merta said.
Employer criticism has rained on Zwickel's idea since he unveiled the plan at a Berlin jobs summit two weeks ago.
Merta also said Germans no longer believed the union's thesis that by cutting back an individual's working hours more jobs could be created by the nation.

In a poll of 1,250 people conducted by the Dimap research institute, 72 percent opposed the introduction of a 32 hour working week while 25 percent said they believed the step would help create new jobs, Bild said.
But IG Metall deputy head Walter Riester told German radio that the plan was an appropriate way to trim the jobless rate.
"By cutting the working week to 35 hours we were able to keep 800,000 people employed," Riester said.
In the late 1980s unions launched a drive to cut hours to give workers more leisure time and IG Metall succeeded in paring its working week back to 35 hours.

The idea of opening up the possibility of creating more jobs seemed like an afterthought. But as Germany's employment problems intensified in the 1990s unions revamped their approach into a strategy to pare jobless rates.

Zwickel, who grabbed headlines with the 32 hour proposal two weeks ago, said in an interview with Der Spiegel union members would only be willing to accept lower wages if employers pledged to create new jobs in return.
